def: Any assisted reproduction technique (artificial insemination, in vitro fertilization) used to control the genetics and productivity of animals.
A Brazilian brand (Life Co) of plant-based creamy requeijão, a spreadable cheese similar to cream cheese, made from soy.
The act of removing an animal from a situation of exploitation, abandonment or risk, usually followed by rehabilitation or adoption.
Recognition of a being's value that guides treatment consistent with its dignity or interests.
com: Extending respect to a being implies recognizing its interests as morally relevant, regardless of its usefulness or its similarity to humans.

def: Forced confrontation between animals (roosters, dogs) for entertainment and betting, usually illegal.
com: In Brazil, the Supreme Federal Court struck down several state laws that authorized cockfighting, such as Rio de Janeiro's in 2011, holding the practice to be cruelty prohibited by the Constitution. In the United States, taking part in animal fighting is a federal crime. Even so, clandestine fights continue to be uncovered, and cockfighting is legal and popular in countries such as the Philippines. See Animal cruelty, The Link and Vaquejada.

def: Risks of suffering on an astronomical scale ("s-risks"), a concept tied to concern about massive future suffering, including that of animals.
Existential risks, capable of extinguishing human life and sentient life or its future potential.
Practices of sacrifice or ritual use, a sensitive topic at the intersection of ethics and religion.
com: The rituals vary widely: they include religious slaughter for food, such as halal and kosher, and sacrifices at festivals and ceremonies of many religions worldwide. In Brazil, the Supreme Federal Court ruled in 2019 that the Rio Grande do Sul law allowing animal sacrifice in Afro-Brazilian religious ceremonies is constitutional. Critics point out that outrage at these rituals is often directed at religious minorities, while the slaughter of billions of animals in ordinary livestock farming receives little attention; from a sentientist point of view, the criterion should be the same in every case: the animal's suffering and death. See Religious speciesism, Selective outrage and Cultural relativism.

def: A spectacle in which horses or bulls are ridden or chased by competitors, involving methods that induce stressful behavior in the animal.
com: In Brazil, Law 10,519/2002 requires cinches and girths of natural wool and bans pointed spurs and electric shocks, but allows the flank strap; in 2016 another law declared rodeo and vaquejada intangible cultural heritage. Animals can suffer fractures and other injuries, and calf-roping events, in which calves are brought down at high speed, are among the most criticized. See Flank strap, Vaquejada and Bullfighting.

def: A tourist activity of observing (or hunting) wild animals in their habitat, with debates about its impact on welfare and conservation.
A sulfurous salt of volcanic or mineral origin, used in vegan cooking to reproduce the taste of egg in recipes.
A nonprofit institution dedicated to taking in and caring for rescued animals, with no purpose of exploitation or commercial breeding.
com: Sanctuaries differ from zoos and breeding facilities because they do not buy, sell or breed the animals, and seek to give them the best possible life until natural death. Because the name is not protected and is also used by places that exploit animals for tourism, with elephant rides or contact with big-cat cubs, organizations such as the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries (GFAS) accredit sanctuaries that meet care standards. Farmed animal sanctuaries also play an educational role, showing pigs, cows and chickens as individuals. See Rescue, Zoo and Adoption.

def: Solid fat extracted from animal tissues, used to make candles, soaps and some foods.
com: Tallow is a by-product of slaughter and appears in little-noticed uses, such as soaps, candles, lubricants and industrial additives. In 2016, the Bank of England confirmed that the new polymer £5 notes contained traces of tallow; a petition against this passed 130,000 signatures, but the bank kept the notes, citing cost. The case shows how animal derivatives circulate in products almost no one associates with animals. See Gelatin and Lanolin.

def: A textile fiber produced by silkworm larvae, whose traditional extraction usually involves killing the larvae inside the cocoon.
com: In conventional production, cocoons are boiled or steamed with the pupa still alive inside, so that the thread can be unwound whole; estimates, mostly from animal protection organizations, range from 5,000 to 7,000 larvae per kilogram of silk. So-called "ahimsa" or "peace" silk waits for the moth to leave the cocoon, but it also draws criticism, for example about rearing conditions. Insect sentience is still debated, but there is growing evidence that some insects can feel pain. See Wool, Fur and leather and Xenospeciesism.

def: Guaranteed regular and permanent access to food of sufficient quality for a healthy life, a topic connected to food justice.
com: The most widely used definition is the one from the FAO World Food Summit of 1996. Animal farming competes with people for land and grain: according to a study by Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek published in *Science* in 2018, animal products take up about 83% of farmland and provide only 18% of the calories eaten worldwide. For this reason, diets with fewer animal products are often pointed to as a way to feed more people on the same land, although hunger depends mainly on income, distribution and conflict. See Food justice, Soy and Food classism.

def: Deliberate human choice of desired genetic traits in animals through controlled breeding.
com: Selection for productivity has changed animals' bodies: according to a 2014 study by Martin Zuidhof and colleagues, broiler growth increased by more than 400% between 1957 and 2005, and rapid growth is associated with leg and heart problems. Dairy cows produce far more milk than the calf needs, which is associated with more mastitis and hoof problems, and laying hens lay about 300 eggs a year, far more than the wild ancestral species. In dogs, selection for appearance has produced hereditary diseases. See Pedigree, Artificial insemination and Domestication.

def: Small reproductive structures of plants, used as food, oil or as the base of plant-based cheeses.
The capacity to feel, to have positive or negative subjective experiences such as pain, pleasure and fear.
com: For sentientism, it is sentience, and not species, intelligence or a being's usefulness to others, that is the only morally relevant criterion for determining who deserves consideration.

termo: Sentience in AI and digital systems
def: The debate over whether artificial systems could develop subjective experience and, if so, deserve moral consideration.
com: A consistent sentientist perspective would require extending moral consideration to these systems once there is sufficient evidence of sentience, regardless of their biological or artificial origin.
pt: Senciência em IA e sistemas digitais

def: A variant of the previous discussion applied to artificial physical bodies; a frontier question in machine ethics.
com: (see the note under Sentience in AI and digital systems)

def: The speculative extension of the moral circle to hypothetical sentient life forms beyond Earth.
com: From a sentientist standpoint, a being's cosmic origin is morally irrelevant: what matters is solely its capacity to suffer or feel pleasure.

def: A position that takes sentience, not species, as the criterion of moral inclusion; also called sentiocentrism.
com: It is the criterion adopted, explicitly or implicitly, in most of the critical remarks in this dictionary.

def: A proposal for political and social organization guided by the interests of all sentient beings.
com: It represents the broadest institutional and political application of sentientism, proposing to extend representation and political participation, today restricted to humans, to all beings capable of having interests.

def: Any being capable of having subjective experiences, positive or negative.
com: It is this category, and not that of "human being" or "intelligent being", that for sentientism correctly delimits the circle of those who deserve moral consideration.

def: Any organism that exhibits biological processes such as metabolism, growth and reproduction; a broader category than "sentient being", since it also includes plants and microorganisms. Not every living being is sentient.
com: This distinction is central to sentientism, which grants direct moral consideration only to beings capable of feeling, which sets it apart from biocentric currents that extend moral value to every form of life.

def: A network of specialized cells (neurons) that allows an organism to process stimuli and coordinate responses; the proposed physiological basis for the capacity to feel.
com: The absence of a nervous system of the known kind in certain species should not, by itself, be taken as proof of the absence of sentience, given how limited scientific knowledge on the subject still is.

def: The part of the nervous system made up of the brain and spinal cord, sometimes used as a criterion for inferring the presence of sentience in a species.
com: Adopting this anatomical criterion exclusively risks underestimating the capacity to feel in species with different nervous architectures, such as octopuses and many insects.

def: A movement that values traditional, local and carefully prepared food, as opposed to fast food.
A set of political currents that advocate collective ownership or control of the means of production and the reduction of class inequalities.
com: Authors such as Ted Benton and David Nibert apply the critique of exploitation and commodification to animals.

def: A negative state experienced by a sentient being, which can include pain, fear, stress, frustration, hunger, boredom or isolation, especially when intense or prolonged.
com: Suffering is broader than physical pain: an animal confined without room to move, separated from their mother or prevented from natural behaviors can suffer without being injured. So the moral question is not only "does it hurt?" but "what is this animal's life like?". See Pain, Animal welfare and Sentience.

def: Pain and death that occur without human intervention (disease, predation, disasters).
com: Most wild animals are born into species that have many offspring, and most of these die shortly after birth from hunger, disease, cold or predation. For this reason some philosophers, such as Oscar Horta, argue that suffering in nature is enormous and deserves moral attention, even without human fault. Others answer that intervening in nature may cause more harm than it prevents; the most common position among those who study the subject is to research before acting. It is also disputed that suffering predominates in nature: Zach Groff and Yew-Kwang Ng (2019) found an error in Ng's 1995 model and concluded that the balance is uncertain, and Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) argue that wild lives may be considerably more positive than assumed; Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that, even with a positive balance, there would still be reasons to help the animals who suffer. See Wild animal suffering, Idyllic nature and Predation.

def: A philosophical debate over whether and how humans would have an obligation to intervene to reduce suffering in nature.
com: In nature, most species have many offspring, and almost all of them die young, from hunger, cold, disease or predation. If suffering matters wherever it occurs, this is also a moral problem. Most of those who study the subject don't propose intervening on a large scale today, for lack of knowledge and the risk of making things worse, but rather researching and acting in safe cases, such as vaccinating wild animals against rabies, rescue in disasters and contraception. See Suffering from natural causes, Idyllic nature and Predation.

def: A versatile legume, the basis of countless vegan products (tofu, milk, soy meat).
com: It is common to hear that vegans' soy destroys forests, but according to Our World in Data, based on FAO data, more than three quarters of the world's soy becomes feed for farmed animals, and only a small part is eaten directly by people, as tofu, soy milk or tempeh. In Brazil, one of the largest producers, soy expansion is linked to deforestation in the Cerrado and the Amazon. People who eat meat generally consume more soy indirectly than people who eat tofu. See Food security, Plant protein and Livestock farming.

def: The degree to which a being is taken into account for its own sake in the ethical decisions of others.
com: For sentientism, a being's moral status derives solely from its capacity to feel, not from its species, intelligence or usefulness to others.

def: The current state of things.
com: Invoking it to justify maintaining practices of animal exploitation is considered by antispeciesists to be a fallacy: the fact that something is customary does not imply that it is morally right.

def: A subculture that emerged from US hardcore punk in the early 1980s, whose followers abstain from alcohol, tobacco and other drugs; the vegan straight edge strand, which spread in the 1990s, adds the refusal of animal products.
com: The name comes from the song "Straight Edge" by the band Minor Threat (1981). Not every straight edger is vegan, and veganism doesn't require abstaining from alcohol: the two choices met in part of the hardcore scene, which helped spread veganism among young people.

def: The condition of being a "subject-of-a-life", with one's own perspective on what happens to one (a central concept in Tom Regan, cited only as a reference).
com: Recognizing a being's subjectivity implies recognizing it as someone, and not as something, a shift in perspective central to overcoming speciesism.

def: The use of animals out of a need for direct survival, a recurring argument in debates about ethical exceptions.
com: The argument applies to real situations, such as peoples living in regions without viable alternatives, and many advocates of veganism recognize these exceptions; the Vegan Society's definition speaks of avoiding exploitation "as far as is possible and practicable". Most consumption of animal products in the world, however, takes place where alternatives exist, and the argument does not extend to those cases. See Necessity, Hunting and Veganism.

def: The position that what matters morally is ensuring that all individuals reach a sufficient minimum threshold of well-being, prioritizing those below that threshold.
com: From this standpoint, ensuring that no animal has its well-being reduced below a minimally acceptable threshold would be morally more urgent than maximizing aggregate well-being or seeking full equality.

def: A concept from Tom Regan (cited only as a reference) designating beings with a unified psychophysical existence, memory, preferences and a well-being of their own, who deserve basic rights.
com: This concept underpins the defense of basic rights, to life and to liberty, for various nonhuman species, and not only for humans.

def: In the livestock context, an identification plate used on animals or rural properties.
A paste made from ground sesame seeds, the base ingredient of hummus.
A fermented soy-based food of Indonesian origin, rich in protein.
The view that God or the divine is the center of reality and morality.
com: Theocentric traditions vary: some see animals as created to serve humans, while others call for compassion and care toward them, as in ahimsa and tza'ar ba'alei chayim.

def: The capacity to attribute mental states to oneself and to others; studied in primates, corvids and cetaceans as an indication of cognitive complexity. Evidence of theory of mind in many species reinforces the idea that cognitive complexity is not exclusively human, undermining one of the traditional arguments of speciesism.
An umbrella term for the set of normative approaches (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, care ethics and others) used to justify moral positions, including on animals.
com: How each of these theories treats, or fails to treat, animals as moral subjects is one of the main axes of comparison among them within animal ethics.

def: The practice of publicly documenting animal suffering at sites of exploitation (slaughterhouses, markets).
com: The practice spread from Toronto Pig Save, founded in Canada in 2010, which inspired hundreds of similar groups known as the Save Movement. In 2017, its founder, Anita Krajnc, was acquitted of charges for giving water to pigs in a truck on the way to slaughter, in a case that drew international attention. See Vigil and Street activism.

def: A food obtained by coagulating soy milk and pressing it into blocks; one of the main sources of vegan protein.
A brand of tofu-based products formulated to imitate turkey meat, associated with vegan festive meals.
A spectacle involving a confrontation between a bull and bullfighters, usually resulting in serious injury and the death of the animal.
com: In the Spanish bullfight, the bull is wounded with lances and banderillas before being killed with a sword; in Portugal, killing in the ring is generally prohibited, but the bull is wounded and usually slaughtered afterwards. Bullfighting is still legal in a few countries, such as Spain, Portugal, France (in some regions), Mexico, Peru, Ecuador and Venezuela, and in 2024 Colombia passed a law banning it from 2027. Supporters invoke tradition and culture, an argument that also appears in defence of vaquejada and rodeo. See Banderillas, Vaquejada and Cultural relativism.

def: The use of an animal's physical strength to pull loads or vehicles.
A labeling warning indicating possible cross-contamination of a product with small unintentional amounts of an ingredient (such as milk or egg).
com: Vegans debate whether a product that "may contain traces of milk" is vegan. The Vegan Society accepts this warning on products with its trademark, as long as the contamination risk is managed, because it signals a risk on the production line, not an ingredient; other certifiers are stricter. The warning exists to protect people with allergies, and avoiding these products does not reduce the use of animals. See Vegan and Cruelty-free.

def: The illegal trade in wild or domestic animals, often involving capture, transport and cruel conditions.
com: In Brazil, Renctas, a network against wildlife trafficking, has estimated since its first report in 2001 that about 38 million wild animals are taken from nature each year, most of them birds, and that most die during capture or transport; the figure is old and its method is poorly documented. In international trade, the CITES convention regulates the sale of endangered species. Trafficking supplies mainly the pet market, as well as collectors, traditional medicine and food, and it increases the risk of zoonoses. See CITES, Pet shop and Zoonosis.

def: A gradual process of changing eating habits, usually toward reducing or eliminating animal products.
A stage of the production chain associated with stress, injuries and mortality.
com: Animals can spend hours or days without food, water or rest, in extreme heat or cold, and many are injured or die on the way. The export of live cattle by ship, on voyages lasting weeks, is especially criticized, and Brazil is one of the major exporters. New Zealand banned the export of farm animals by sea in 2023, and the United Kingdom banned live exports for slaughter and fattening in 2024. See Live cargo, Downed animal and Slaughter.

def: A person responsible for the care of a companion animal; a term preferred by activists over "owner", because it does not imply a property relationship.
The practice of taking on continuing responsibility for the care of an animal, usually a rescued one, as an alternative to the concept of ownership.
com: Replacing "owner" with "guardian" shows a change of outlook, but in the law of most countries animals are still property. Some countries changed the status of animals in their civil codes, such as France in 2015, Portugal in 2017 and Spain in 2021, which now recognize them as sentient beings, without giving them full legal personhood. See Guardian or caregiver, Animals as property and Animal legal personhood.

def: The principle that valid moral judgments must apply equally to all relevantly similar cases, regardless of who carries them out.
com: It is the logical basis of the argument from marginal cases and of much of the antispeciesist critique: if a moral criterion holds for humans in a given situation, it must hold equally for animals in a relevantly similar situation.

def: A consequentialist strand that seeks to maximize well-being and minimize the aggregate suffering of those affected by a decision (reference: Bentham, Singer, cited only as examples).
com: Bentham already pointed out, as early as the eighteenth century, that the relevant question about animals is not whether they can reason or talk, but whether they can suffer, a seminal formulation of sentientism.

def: The version of utilitarianism that seeks to maximize the total aggregate sum of well-being of all those affected by a decision, without giving additional weight to those who are worse off.
com: It differs from negative utilitarianism in holding that positive experiences can, in principle, compensate for suffering.

def: A variant of utilitarianism whose goal is to minimize the total aggregate of suffering, holding that no amount of positive well-being can compensate for it. This variant tends to give stronger moral priority to eliminating animal suffering than to promoting positive experiences, which brings it closer to more urgent positions within the animal liberation movement.
The value attributed to something because of its usefulness for another end, and not for its own sake.
com: Treating animals exclusively as bearers of instrumental value, as resources, is the core of the abolitionist and antispeciesist critique of their status as property.

def: The value a being has in itself, regardless of its usefulness to others; also called value in itself or inherent value.
com: It is the central concept of animal rights theories, which hold that every subject-of-a-life has intrinsic value, incompatible with being treated as a mere resource.

def: A traditional Brazilian practice in which two cowboys on horseback chase a bull and bring it down by the tail, causing physical injuries to the animal.
com: In 2016, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court struck down a law from the state of Ceará regulating vaquejada, finding that the practice subjects animals to cruelty, which the Constitution forbids. In 2017, Congress passed Constitutional Amendment 96, which states that sporting practices with animals registered as cultural expressions are not considered cruel. The case shows the conflict between tradition and animal protection, and how the law can be changed to keep a practice going. See Rodeo, Bullfighting and Animal cruelty.

def: The use of vegan or plant-based imagery by brands or companies with no real commitment to the animal cause.
com: It is criticized for diluting the ethical meaning of veganism, reducing it to a market trend detached from the moral consideration for animals that originally motivates it.

def: A philosophy and practice that seeks to exclude, as far as possible and practicable, all forms of animal exploitation.
com: The most cited definition is that of the Vegan Society, founded in England in 1944. Veganism is not only a diet: it includes clothing, entertainment, testing and other uses. The phrase "as far as is possible and practicable" acknowledges that living without causing any harm to animals is impossible, and also opens debates about where that limit lies, for example with medicines tested on animals. There is disagreement about whether veganism is a moral baseline, as abolitionism holds, or a means of reducing suffering, as pragmatic strands hold. See Vegan, Vegan diet, Abolitionist veganism and Pragmatic veganism.

def: A strand that emphasizes ending animals' status as property as its central axis, critical of welfarism.
com: This strand is associated with the legal scholar Gary Francione, who defends veganism as a moral baseline and vegan education as the main strategy, and criticizes welfare reform campaigns and single-issue campaigns. Critics accuse it of purism and say it rejects concrete gains for animals alive today. See Abolitionism, Welfarism and Pragmatic veganism.

def: A strand that links veganism with a critique of patriarchal structures (connected to ecofeminism).
com: The best-known work is *The Sexual Politics of Meat* (1990) by Carol J. Adams, which links the objectification of women and of animals and proposed the idea of the absent referent. The strand also draws attention to the exploitation of females' reproductive systems, as in milk and egg production. See Ecofeminism, Absent referent and Dairy products.

def: A strand of veganism that links the defense of animals to fighting other forms of oppression, such as racism, sexism, class inequality and ableism.
com: In practice, this means, for example, considering slaughterhouse workers, who are among the most exploited in the food chain; working so that plant-based food is affordable to people who are poor or live on the margins; fighting racism and sexism within the movement itself; and avoiding comparisons and campaigns that offend historically oppressed groups. There is a debate about the limits: part of the movement fears the animal cause will be diluted across many causes, and another part points out that excluding people drives allies away. This guide doesn't require every vegan to embrace every cause, but asks that no one use the animal cause to harm other groups, and that no one use other causes to dismiss the animals. See Intersectionality, Afro-veganism (or Black veganism), Working-class veganism (veganismo popular, Brazilian usage), Ecofeminism and Instrumentalization.

def: A strand aimed at the economic and cultural accessibility of veganism for working-class communities.
A strand focused on results and harm reduction, prioritizing mass adoption over ideological purity.
A diet that excludes the meat of any animal, including fish and seafood; in the strict sense, it also excludes all other animal products, such as milk, eggs and honey.
com: The word has two senses. In the broad sense (lato sensu), the most common, a vegetarian is someone who doesn't eat meat but may consume milk, eggs or honey; in practice, most are lacto-ovo vegetarians, and that is what most people understand by the term. In the strict sense (stricto sensu), vegetarianism is a diet free of all animal products, which in Brazil is called strict vegetarianism. Those who defend the strict sense often say it was the original meaning, and there is some support for this: some of the first to use the word, in the early 1840s, such as the members of the Alcott House community in England, ate no animal products at all. But the Vegetarian Society, founded in 1847 and responsible for popularizing the term, accepted eggs and dairy from the start, and that usage took hold; historians still debate the exact meaning of the earliest records. It was to name those who consumed no animal products that the word vegan was coined in 1944. Many people think vegetarians eat fish, but they don't, and some products hide ingredients from dead animals, such as gelatin and the rennet in certain cheeses. See Vegetarian, Strict vegetarianism, Lacto-ovo vegetarianism and Veganism.

def: A diet free of all animal products: no meat, fish, seafood, milk and dairy, eggs or honey.
com: It corresponds to the strict sense of vegetarianism and is the expression used in Brazil, for example by the Brazilian Vegetarian Society. It describes only the diet: veganism includes the same diet, but goes further and rejects animal exploitation also in clothing, entertainment and other uses. See Vegetarianism, Vegan diet and Veganism.

def: The medical science dedicated to the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of diseases, trauma and disorders in animals.
com: Historically, because much of its practice is oriented toward animal exploitation and productivity, the field is in tension with welfare approaches and non-anthropocentric worldviews.

def: A current that discusses the moral dilemmas of veterinary practice, such as euthanasia, the use of animals in livestock farming and experimentation.
com: One of its central dilemmas is the fact that a good part of veterinary professionals work directly in the service of animal exploitation systems, which creates conflict between the duty of care and the economic function of the work.

def: Systematic distortions of judgment that affect how animal suffering is perceived. Biases such as cognitive dissonance and conformity bias help explain why widely shared beliefs about the moral value of animals do not always translate into consistent behavior.
An essential nutrient produced by microorganisms, not reliably present in plant sources, whose supplementation is usually recommended in vegan diets.
com: B12 is not produced by animals or plants, but by bacteria. In livestock farming, farmed animals are usually given cobalt or B12 itself in their feed, so part of the B12 in meat also comes from supplements. For this reason, the need to supplement does not show that a vegan diet is unnatural, only that the source of the vitamin has changed. See Vegan diet and Nutritional yeast.

def: Meat from calves slaughtered while still young, often raised in intensive confinement (the veal crate).
com: Veal is a by-product of the dairy industry: male calves of dairy breeds do not produce milk and grow too slowly for beef production, so they are killed young, at days, weeks or a few months of age. Traditional pale meat depends on a low-iron diet and little movement. Even where veal crates have been banned, as in the European Union, separation from the mother and slaughter at a young age continue. See Veal crate, Dairy industry and Premature slaughter.

def: Experimentation on live animals, a historically loaded term used by antivivisection movements.

Moral discrimination among different nonhuman species, privileging some (e.g. dogs, dolphins) over others (e.g. insects, fish) without a morally relevant justification. It is pointed out by sentientists as a "second-degree" form of speciesism: even among those who already reject human superiority, aesthetic preferences or preferences based on similarity end up recreating morally arbitrary hierarchies among nonhuman species.
The transplantation of organs or tissues between different species (e.g. from pigs to humans), raising ethical questions about the use of animals as "organ banks".
com: The organs come from genetically modified pigs, raised in isolated facilities and killed to remove their organs. The first pig heart transplants into living patients, in the United States in 2022 and 2023, gave survival of at most about two months; pig kidney transplants performed since 2024 have had better results, and the FDA authorized clinical trials in 2025. The shortage of human organs is real, but critics argue that the technique expands the use of animals as a source of spare parts and advocate strengthening human organ donation and other alternatives. See Genetic engineering, Animal experimentation and Instrumentalization.

def: A film that forms on the surface of heated soy milk, used as food in Asian cuisine.

A psychological state of familiarity and low risk that tends to resist change. In the context of animal consumption, it is often cited as one of the main psychological obstacles to adopting habits more aligned with the equal consideration of interests across species.
The practice of sexual activity between humans and animals; a crime and a serious form of animal abuse.
The branch of biology dedicated to the scientific study of animals.
com: Like ethology, zoology has helped dismantle traditional hierarchies among species by revealing the biological and behavioral complexity of organisms once considered "inferior".

def: An institution that keeps wild animals in captivity for display, education or research; a central target of criticism by the animal liberation movement.
com: Zoos are justified by conservation and education, but many of the species on display are not threatened, and it is hard to show that visits change the public's behavior. Animals that range over large areas in the wild, such as elephants, polar bears and big cats, tend to suffer more in captivity, with stereotypies and higher mortality. Zoos differ, and some are closer to rescue centers or sanctuaries. See Captive breeding, Environmental enrichment and Sanctuary.

def: An infectious disease that passes from other animals to humans, or the other way round.
com: Most infectious diseases that emerge in humans originate in animals: a study published in *Nature* in 2008 found that 60% of emerging disease events between 1940 and 2004 were zoonoses, and that 72% of these came from wildlife, such as HIV and Ebola. Intensive farming, with thousands of genetically similar animals kept close together, favours the circulation and mutation of viruses, such as those of bird flu and swine flu; the wildlife trade, hunting and deforestation also increase contact between species. See Pandemic, Antimicrobial resistance, Industrial livestock farming and Animal trafficking.

def: Pleasure derived from inflicting suffering or death on animals; a form of cruelty associated with behavioral disorders.

A science applied to the breeding and management of animals for production, historically oriented toward productivity and economic yield. Because it defines animals primarily as productive resources, zootechnics is often pointed to by abolitionist currents as a structurally speciesist discipline, even when it incorporates welfare parameters.
